OPERATING SYSTEM
CONCEPTS AND FUNCTIONS

Digital Learning Book

Book Introduction

An operating system (OS) is the foundational software that makes a computer or digital device usable. It coordinates the processor, memory, storage, input and output devices, and applications. It provides services that allow programs to run, data to be organized, users to interact with the system, and resources to be shared safely.

Operating systems are present in personal computers, smartphones, servers, embedded controllers, and cloud environments. Their responsibilities include process management, memory management, file systems, device control, security, networking, and system monitoring. Although these functions may seem separate, they work together to make computing reliable and convenient.

This e-book introduces operating-system concepts from a practical, student-friendly perspective. It begins with the purpose and structure of an OS, then explores processes, memory, files, I/O, security, and modern platform features. Examples use familiar devices and situations.

The chapters combine detailed explanations, text illustrations, practical applications, review questions, and activities. The goal is to understand how an operating system coordinates a complete computer system rather than merely memorize technical terms.

General Learning Objectives

- After completing this e-book, learners should be able to:

- Define an operating system and explain its purpose.

- Identify major operating-system components and services.

- Describe process, thread, and CPU scheduling concepts.

- Explain memory allocation, paging, virtual memory, and page replacement.

- Describe file-system organization and storage management.

- Explain device drivers, interrupts, buffering, and DMA.

- Recognize operating-system security and protection mechanisms.

- Compare operating-system types and modern deployment environments.

- Apply OS concepts to troubleshooting and practical computing scenarios.

- Use technical vocabulary accurately in diagrams and written explanations.

Chapter 1 — Introduction to Operating Systems

Learning objectives

- Define an operating system.

- Identify major OS responsibilities.

- Explain how an OS supports applications and users.

1.1 What is an Operating System?

An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware and provides common services to application programs. It acts as an intermediary between users, applications, and physical resources such as the CPU, RAM, storage, display, keyboard, and network interface.

Without an OS, each application would need to manage hardware directly. This would make programs more complex, difficult to maintain, and likely to interfere with one another. The OS creates a consistent environment in which multiple applications can run and share resources.

For example, when a student saves a document, the word processor requests a file operation. The OS checks access permissions, coordinates the file system, communicates with storage drivers, and manages the transfer of data to the storage device.

1.2 Main Goals of an Operating System

Convenience: provide a usable environment for people and applications.

Efficiency: use CPU, memory, and devices effectively.

Reliability: detect and handle errors and keep the system stable.

Protection: prevent unauthorized access to resources.

Security: defend data and services against threats.

Extensibility: support new hardware, features, and applications.

1.3 Core Functions

The OS manages processes and threads, allocates memory, organizes files, controls I/O devices, enforces access controls, and offers interfaces for applications. It also supports communication, error reporting, and system configuration.

These functions are interconnected. A browser needs CPU time to execute, memory to store active pages, file access to cache data, and network I/O to retrieve content. The OS coordinates these requests while allowing other programs to operate.

1.4 User Interface and Applications

A graphical user interface (GUI) uses windows, icons, menus, and pointers. A command-line interface (CLI) accepts typed commands. Both provide ways to request operating-system services. Applications such as word processors, games, and browsers are not themselves operating systems; they run on top of one.

Text illustration: USER → APPLICATION → OPERATING SYSTEM → HARDWARE. The OS manages the hardware resources and offers controlled services to the application.

1.5 Practical Application

When several applications are open, the OS shares processor time, tracks their memory, responds to keyboard and mouse events, and manages file access. If one application stops responding, the OS may allow the user to terminate that process without restarting the entire computer.

Chapter 2 — OS Structure, Services, and System Calls

Learning objectives

- Describe kernel and user mode.

- Explain system calls and OS services.

- Compare common OS architecture approaches.

2.1 The Kernel

The kernel is the central part of an operating system. It executes with privileged access and handles essential operations such as scheduling, memory management, device interaction, and system-call processing. Other OS components may run as services or utilities outside the kernel.

User applications normally execute in user mode, where access to protected hardware and memory is restricted. Kernel mode permits privileged operations. This separation helps prevent ordinary programs from directly damaging the system.

2.2 System Calls and OS Services

A system call is a controlled request from an application to the OS kernel. Common examples include creating a process, opening a file, allocating memory, or communicating through a network socket. The kernel validates the request and performs the service according to system rules.

System services may include program execution, I/O operations, file manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting, and protection.

2.3 OS Architecture

A monolithic kernel places many OS services in kernel space. This can reduce communication overhead, but a large privileged code base can be difficult to isolate. A microkernel keeps the kernel small and moves more services into user space; this can improve modularity, although communication between components may add overhead.

Layered systems organize OS functions into levels, each using services from lower layers. Hybrid designs combine elements from several approaches. Real operating systems often use practical mixtures rather than one perfectly pure model.

2.4 Interrupts and Exceptions

An interrupt signals an event that needs attention, such as a device completing an operation. An exception is associated with the currently executing instruction, such as an invalid operation or a memory-access fault. The processor transfers control to a handler, which deals with the event and may resume or terminate execution.

Chapter 3 — Operating-System Types and Design Approaches

3.1 Batch, Multiprogramming, and Time-Sharing Systems

Batch systems collect jobs and execute them with limited direct interaction. Multiprogramming keeps several jobs in memory so the CPU can work on another job while one waits for I/O. Time-sharing systems rapidly switch CPU attention among tasks or users to provide interactive responsiveness.

3.2 Real-Time Systems

Real-time systems are designed around timing constraints. A hard real-time system must meet specified critical deadlines; a missed deadline may constitute system failure. A soft real-time system can tolerate occasional missed deadlines, though service quality may decline. Examples include industrial control, multimedia, and monitoring systems.

3.3 Distributed, Network, and Embedded Systems

Network operating systems support communication and resource sharing among connected computers. Distributed systems coordinate multiple machines and may present resources as a unified service. Embedded operating systems support dedicated devices with constraints involving power, memory, cost, or predictable timing.

3.4 Desktop, Server, and Mobile OSs

Desktop OSs emphasize interactive applications and broad peripheral support. Server OSs focus on service availability, networking, security, and remote management. Mobile OSs integrate touch interaction, sensors, wireless communication, power management, and application permission models.

Chapter 4 — Processes and Threads

Learning objectives

- Distinguish programs, processes, and threads.

- Describe process states and process control blocks.

- Explain context switching and concurrency.

4.1 Program versus Process

A program is a passive set of instructions stored in a file. A process is a program in execution, including its current state, memory, resources, and execution context. Multiple processes may run instances of the same program while maintaining separate state.

The OS tracks a process using a process control block (PCB). A PCB commonly records a process identifier, state, register context, scheduling information, memory information, and resource references.

4.2 Process States

A simplified state model includes NEW, READY, RUNNING, WAITING, and TERMINATED. A newly created process becomes ready when eligible to run. The scheduler dispatches a ready process to the CPU. A running process may wait for I/O, return to ready after preemption, or terminate when finished.

4.3 Threads and Context Switching

A thread is an execution path within a process. Threads in the same process typically share code, data, and open resources, but each thread has its own stack and execution state. Threads can improve responsiveness and allow parallel work on multicore processors.

A context switch saves the state of one process or thread and restores another. Switching enables multitasking but consumes time and may disturb caches. It is necessary for sharing processor resources among competing tasks.

4.4 Concurrency and Parallelism

Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress during overlapping periods. Parallelism means tasks execute at the same instant on separate execution resources. Concurrent programs require coordination when they share data. Synchronization mechanisms such as locks, semaphores, and condition variables help prevent race conditions.

Chapter 5 — CPU Scheduling and Synchronization

5.1 Scheduling Goals

CPU scheduling selects a ready process or thread to execute. Common goals include high CPU utilization and throughput, low waiting and response time, fairness, and respect for priority or deadline constraints. Different systems emphasize different goals.

5.2 Scheduling Algorithms

First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): runs tasks in arrival order; simple but can produce long waits.

Shortest Job First (SJF): selects the shortest expected CPU burst; can minimize average waiting time when estimates are accurate.

Priority scheduling: chooses tasks by priority; aging can reduce starvation.

Round Robin (RR): gives each ready task a time quantum, then cycles to the next; often useful for interactive systems.

Example: P1 requires 5 ms and P2 requires 3 ms, both arriving together. With Round Robin quantum 2 ms, the sequence is P1(2), P2(2), P1(2), P2(1), P1(1).

5.3 Synchronization

A race condition occurs when the result depends on the timing of concurrent operations. A critical section is code that accesses shared state and must be protected. Mutual exclusion ensures only one participating thread enters a protected section at a time.

A deadlock can occur when processes wait indefinitely for resources held by one another. Deadlock analysis commonly considers mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

Chapter 6 — Main-Memory Management

6.1 Memory Management Purpose

Main memory holds instructions and data currently in use. The OS allocates memory to processes, tracks available regions, and enforces protection. Efficient memory management supports multiple applications while limiting interference between them.

6.2 Contiguous Allocation and Fragmentation

Contiguous allocation gives a process one continuous region of physical memory. External fragmentation occurs when free memory is divided into separated holes. Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block. Allocation strategies may include first fit, best fit, and worst fit.

6.3 Paging Basics

Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames. A page table maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers. Paging avoids external fragmentation, though the last page allocated to a process may contain unused space.

6.4 Memory Protection

Memory protection restricts which addresses a process may access and whether it may read, write, or execute them. Hardware mechanisms and OS policy cooperate to enforce boundaries. Protection supports stability because one application should not freely overwrite another application’s memory.

Chapter 7 — Virtual Memory and Paging

7.1 Virtual Memory

Virtual memory gives each process an address space that is mapped to physical memory. It supports isolation and flexible allocation and can allow programs to use more address space than available RAM by keeping some pages on storage.

7.2 Demand Paging and Page Faults

Demand paging loads a page when it is first needed. A page fault occurs when a process references a page that is not currently resident or when an access violates the page’s permissions. For a valid nonresident page, the OS locates the page, obtains a frame, loads data, updates mappings, and resumes the instruction.

7.3 Page Replacement

When no free frame is available, the OS may evict a page. FIFO replaces the page that entered memory earliest. LRU replaces the least recently used page. Optimal replacement evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future and is primarily a theoretical benchmark.

Excessive page faults can cause thrashing, in which the system spends much of its time moving pages rather than executing useful work. Adequate memory and locality-aware workloads help avoid this condition.

7.4 TLB and Translation

A translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches recent virtual-to-physical address translations. A TLB hit can avoid a page-table walk. On a miss, the processor or OS obtains the translation from page tables and may update the TLB.

Chapter 8 — File-System Management

8.1 Files and Directories

A file is a named collection of data. File metadata may include size, timestamps, owner, permissions, and storage location. Directories organize files into a hierarchy. Paths identify locations, such as /home/student/notes.txt or C:\\Users\\Student\\notes.txt.

8.2 File Operations and Access Methods

Typical file operations include create, open, read, write, append, rename, close, and delete. Sequential access processes data in order; direct access allows a program to seek to a selected location. The OS checks permissions and coordinates storage access.

8.3 File-System Structure and Reliability

A file system maps logical file names and offsets to physical storage blocks. Allocation methods include contiguous, linked, and indexed allocation. Journaling file systems record intended metadata changes to help recover consistency after a crash. Journaling is not a substitute for backup.

Access controls determine who may read, modify, or execute files. A reliable backup plan keeps copies separate from the original device and tests restoration. A common guideline is to maintain multiple copies on different media, with one copy off-site or isolated.

Chapter 9 — I/O Systems and Device Management

9.1 Devices and Drivers

A device controller operates hardware, while a device driver is software that enables the OS to communicate with it. Drivers translate OS requests into device-specific operations. Standard interfaces allow applications to use devices without knowing every hardware detail.

9.2 Programmed I/O, Interrupts, and DMA

Programmed I/O makes the CPU repeatedly check device status or move data. Interrupt-driven I/O lets a device notify the CPU when service is needed. Direct Memory Access (DMA) allows a controller to transfer blocks between a device and memory with limited CPU involvement.

DMA is useful for high-volume transfers, such as storage and networking. The CPU configures the operation and the controller performs the transfer; completion may be reported through an interrupt.

9.3 Buffering, Caching, and Spooling

A buffer temporarily holds data during transfer. A cache stores copies of data likely to be reused. Spooling queues jobs for a device, such as print jobs, so applications can continue while the device works. These techniques improve coordination between components with different speeds.

Chapter 10 — Storage, Reliability, and Recovery

10.1 Storage Technologies

Hard disk drives (HDDs) store data magnetically on rotating media and use mechanical movement. Solid-state drives (SSDs) use flash memory and have no moving parts. SSDs typically provide lower access latency, while HDDs may offer economical high capacity. Storage selection depends on workload, durability, capacity, and cost.

10.2 File Systems and Storage Organization

File systems organize data and metadata on storage devices. Examples include NTFS, exFAT, ext4, and APFS. Features vary and may include journaling, snapshots, encryption, checksums, or access controls. Compatibility should be checked when moving storage between systems.

10.3 RAID and Backup

RAID combines storage devices to improve performance, availability, or both through striping, mirroring, or parity. RAID does not replace backup: it may not protect against accidental deletion, malware, theft, or site-wide damage.

A backup strategy considers frequency, retention, separate copies, and restore testing. The value of a backup is demonstrated by successful recovery, not merely by the existence of a copy.

Chapter 11 — Protection, Security, and Users

11.1 Protection and Access Control

Protection controls how users and processes access resources. Authentication verifies identity; authorization determines which actions are allowed. Least privilege means giving each account or process only the access required for its task.

11.2 Common Threats

Malware: harmful software, including viruses, worms, ransomware, and spyware.

Phishing: deceptive messages designed to obtain credentials or sensitive information.

Privilege escalation: gaining permissions beyond those intended.

Unpatched vulnerabilities: weaknesses that remain after fixes are available.

Unauthorized access: use of systems or data without permission.

11.3 Security Practices

Use unique passwords and multifactor authentication, install updates, enable firewall protections, restrict administrator access, encrypt sensitive data, and maintain protected backups. Avoid running unknown software with elevated privileges. Security is a continuing process involving technology, configuration, and user behavior.

Chapter 12 — Networking, Virtualization, and Containers

12.1 OS Networking Services

An OS commonly provides network protocol implementations, socket interfaces, configuration tools, and access controls. Applications use sockets to exchange data. The OS handles communication with network hardware and protocol processing.

12.2 Virtual Machines and Containers

A virtual machine (VM) emulates a computer environment and runs a guest OS on virtual hardware managed by a hypervisor. Containers isolate applications while sharing the host OS kernel. VMs often provide a separate guest operating system; containers are typically lighter and start faster, but use a different isolation boundary.

12.3 Modern Operating-System Environments

Cloud and data-center platforms use operating systems to manage large-scale compute, memory, storage, and networking. Mobile systems emphasize power and permissions. Embedded and real-time systems may prioritize predictable behavior, low resource use, and reliability.

Chapter 13 — Booting, Troubleshooting, and Maintenance

13.1 The Boot Process

A simplified startup sequence is: power on → firmware (BIOS/UEFI) performs checks → selects a boot device → loads a bootloader → bootloader loads the kernel → kernel initializes memory and drivers → system services start → login or user interface appears. Exact details vary by platform.

13.2 Troubleshooting Approach

Record the symptom and exact error message.

Check power, cables, peripherals, network, and available storage.

Save work and restart when appropriate.

Use built-in diagnostics, logs, and process or resource monitors.

Update software and drivers from trusted sources.

Back up important data before risky repair steps.

Change one setting at a time and document the result.

13.3 Maintenance

Keep the OS updated, remove unnecessary startup applications, monitor storage and resource usage, scan for threats, and periodically test backups. Avoid deleting system files or changing advanced settings without understanding their purpose.

Conclusion

Operating systems make computing practical by coordinating hardware, applications, and users. Process scheduling, memory management, file systems, device control, networking, and security are not isolated features; they form a connected system that supports reliable and efficient work.

Understanding these concepts helps learners explain everyday computer behavior, evaluate platforms, troubleshoot common problems, and make informed decisions about security and resource use. As platforms continue to evolve, the fundamental role of the operating system remains the same: manage complexity and provide a dependable environment for computation.
